newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Struggle expected over S.Korean financial reform.
newsitem.headline: Struggle expected over S.Korean financial reform.

text.p: The government of South Korean President Kim Young-sam, battling striking workers over labour reform, will also face a struggle to implement the financial restructuring needed to boost a sagging economy, analysts said.

President Kim said last week the heavily-controlled financial sector urgently needed reform to bring it line with global trends. He said a Committee for Financial Reform would be set up to draft proposals aimed at improving competitiveness.
But analysts said at the weekend Kim would face stiff opposition from powerful bureaucrats.

"All-mighty government officials will not give up their control easily," said Koo Kyung-hoi, a senior economist at Dongwon Economic Research Institute. Lee Hahn-ku, president of the Daewoo Research Institute, said: "Financial reforms have been a buzzword since Kim's inauguration in 1993. But the refreshed call for reform shows Kim has done little so far to improve the financial industry."

Government officials said initial measures, including a cut in rediscount rates, would be taken to lower interest rates and later more sweeping steps would be implemented, such as the scaling-back of business barriers among financial institutions.
Economists have said mergers and aquisitions in the financial sector would eventually be allowed to assist a further market opening.
President Kim said the committee would draw up a short-term reform plan by the end of March and a medium- and long-term plan at the end of the year.

In 1993, the Finance Ministry revealed a comprehensive schedule of reform, giving greater autonomy to banking institutions to enable them to become more competitive. But not much has been accomplished since then, analysts said.
"Banks continue to be remote-controlled by the ministry and forced to be responsible for the failure of the non-financial companies," said Yoon Suk-hun, an economist at Korea Institute of Finance.
As a result, banks have been saddled with mounting non-performing loans. No figures were immediately available.
The government's control over the financial sector stems from the 1960s when South Korea channelled cash it raised overseas to industries deemed strategic to national development through banks.

South Korea has been under international pressure to liberalise its financial regulations to allow more foreign investment on the stock market, which plunged last year during an economic slowdown prompted by falling export growth.

A Daewoo Research Institute report said the economic growth rate would slow to 5.5 percent this year from an originally forecast 5.9 percent if production losses from strikes over a controversial new labour law match those of 1989.
The economy grew an estimated seven percent in 1996.

Official figures released on Saturday show production losses due to three-week old strikes against the forced passage of a new labour law have mounted to $2 billion and export losses are at $345 million.
The new law allows companies to lay off workers and hire temporary staff to break strikes, shattering a jobs-for-life tradition in South Korea.
